explanations.explanation: Egypt is right, baker. Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, was the one he ran from. A man who ran that far doesn't come back for nothing, and I think people were about to notice.

Assyria is a long way off from this story, friend. The text says Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, was the king he ran from. Egypt is the place to remember on this one.

Moab is a good guess if you're picking a faraway place, but it's not this one. The text says Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon was Israel's king and David's son. Jeroboam's hideout was Egypt.

explanations.answer: Lighten the burden his father put on them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They said, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service…” (2 Chronicles 10:4). A yoke is the wooden beam an ox wears to pull a load, so they're talking about heavy work. And they made a promise too: “…and we will serve you.” That's a pretty fair deal.

explanations.answer: Build them a new city in the north
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks for a new city here, friend. The people said, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service…” (2 Chronicles 10:4). A yoke is the beam an ox wears to pull a heavy load. Their request was about lighter work, not new buildings.

explanations.answer: Lead them to war against their enemies
explanations.explanation: No war talk here, baker. The people asked Rehoboam to “…lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us…” (2 Chronicles 10:4). A yoke is the beam an ox wears to pull a heavy load. They wanted relief from the work, and they said they would serve him if he gave it.

I see why you'd think so, friend, but it's False. The people said, “…you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” (2 Chronicles 10:4). They put an offer on the table: lighter work, and they would serve him. That's a request with a promise attached, not a warning.

False is right, baker. The people said, “…you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” (2 Chronicles 10:4). They ask for lighter work and promise to serve him if he does it. That's not a threat. It's a deal waiting for a yes.

explanations.answer: The elders who had served Solomon
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime (2 Chronicles 10:6). Solomon was David's son and Israel's king before him. These men had watched the old king work up close. I'd say that's a good first phone call.

explanations.answer: The priests who served at the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests are a nice guess, friend, but the text doesn't send him to them. Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime (2 Chronicles 10:6). Solomon was Israel's king before him. Those elders are the ones he asked first.

explanations.answer: The prophets who served the LORD
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say he went to the prophets, baker. It says Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime (2 Chronicles 10:6). Solomon was Israel's king before him. The elders were his first stop.

Kind it is, baker. The elders said, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (2 Chronicles 10:7). Notice they say kind twice. When advice repeats a word, I'd write that word on my apron.

Stern is the opposite of what the elders said, friend. They told him, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (2 Chronicles 10:7). Kind words was their advice. Stern talk shows up later, and it comes from somewhere else.

Few is a fair guess, since short answers can be smart. But the elders said, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (2 Chronicles 10:7). They weren't talking about how many words. They were talking about kind ones.

True, baker. The elders said, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (2 Chronicles 10:7). That's a big promise from some seasoned advisors. Kind words on one side, servants forever on the other.

This one is True, friend. The elders said, “If you will be kind to these people and please them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (2 Chronicles 10:7). They said it plainly. Pleasing the people and speaking kindly came with that promise.

explanations.answer: The young men who grew up with him
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him (2 Chronicles 10:8). They'd known him for years. I think that's the kind of crowd that tells you what you want to hear.

No army commanders in this scene, friend. The text says Rehoboam consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him (2 Chronicles 10:8). These were his old companions. That's who he asked after the elders.

Jeroboam is in the story, baker, but he's not the one giving advice. Jeroboam, who had fled from Solomon, is on the other side with the people. Rehoboam consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him (2 Chronicles 10:8). That's who he asked next.

Yes, baker. The young men said to tell them, “Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke.” (2 Chronicles 10:11). The people asked for a lighter load and the advice was a heavier one. That's the opposite of what they wanted, and it's not even close.

If only, friend. The young men told him to say, “Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke.” (2 Chronicles 10:11). Adding to the yoke means making the load heavier. Lifting it off was never part of their advice.

explanations.answer: He will leave it as it is
explanations.explanation: Leaving it alone would have been gentler, baker. But the young men said to tell the people, “Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke.” (2 Chronicles 10:11). They didn't suggest keeping it the same. They suggested adding more.

God is right, baker. The text says, “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God…” (2 Chronicles 10:15). So there's more going on here than a king who wouldn't listen. I'll just say that part plainly and let it be.

The elders were the ones who gave the kind advice, friend, and Rehoboam rejected it (2 Chronicles 10:13). The text says, “…indeed this turn of events was from God…” (2 Chronicles 10:15). So the answer is God, not the elders.

The Philistines aren't anywhere in this scene, baker. The text says, “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God…” (2 Chronicles 10:15). God is the answer. Nobody from outside walked in to change the story.

Right, baker. The text says this was “…in order that the LORD might fulfill the word that He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.” (2 Chronicles 10:15). Ahijah's word came to the very man standing in that crowd. Jeroboam was the one it was spoken to.

Nathan was a prophet, friend, but he's not the one in this verse. The text says the word was spoken “…through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.” (2 Chronicles 10:15). So the word went to Jeroboam, who is right there in this scene.

Iddo the seer is a good guess if you like the prophet names, baker, but the text points somewhere else. It says the word was spoken “…through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.” (2 Chronicles 10:15). Jeroboam is the one who received it.

explanations.answer: Turn from David’s house and go home
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They said, “To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, O David!” and “…all the Israelites went home…” (2 Chronicles 10:16). They said it and then they walked. The conversation was over.

explanations.answer: Stay and plead with the king again
explanations.explanation: They don't plead again, friend. After they spoke, “…all the Israelites went home…” (2 Chronicles 10:16). Their words were “To your tents, O Israel!” and they left. The asking was done.

explanations.answer: Ask for three more days to decide
explanations.explanation: Three days already came and went, baker (2 Chronicles 10:12). This time they didn't ask for more. They said, “To your tents, O Israel!” and “…all the Israelites went home…” (2 Chronicles 10:16).

True, baker. The text says, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 10:17). Most of Israel walked away, but he still had a kingdom to rule. It was smaller than before.

It's True, friend. The text says, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 10:17). Israel went home, but Judah's cities were still his. That's a smaller kingdom, but he was still king.

explanations.answer: Flees in his chariot to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, “And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 10:18). In haste, no speeches. A few days ago this man was telling people his little finger was thicker than his father's waist, and now he's leaving fast.

explanations.answer: Calls the elders back for advice
explanations.explanation: He doesn't call the elders back, friend. The text says, “And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 10:18). He left in a hurry. There wasn't time for another round of advice.

explanations.answer: Goes out to speak with the crowd
explanations.explanation: No more talking with the crowd, baker. They had just stoned Hadoram to death, and the text says, “And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 10:18). It's a heavy moment, and he got out of there fast.
